clinicalPearls: Benign bony outgrowths of the external auditory canal, usually multiple and bilateral, caused by repeated exposure to cold water and wind
It is strongly associated with cold-water surfing, diving and swimming, hence the term surfer's ear
Many are asymptomatic, but narrowing predisposes to trapped water, wax impaction and recurrent otitis externa
Progressive canal occlusion can cause conductive hearing loss
A solitary bony lesion is more likely an osteoma, which differs in pathology and distribution
Water precautions slow progression, and surgery is reserved for significant obstruction or recurrent infection
reference.pathophysiology: External auditory canal exostoses are broad-based bony overgrowths arising from the tympanic bone of the canal in response to repeated cold-water and wind exposure. The chronic thermal stimulation is thought to provoke periosteal bone formation, producing progressive concentric narrowing of the bony canal. The narrowed, tortuous canal traps water and cerumen, impairing self-cleaning and predisposing to external ear infection and, when severe, conductive hearing loss.
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy demonstrating the characteristic bony narrowing
Audiometry if conductive hearing loss is suspected
CT of the temporal bone before surgery to define the bony anatomy
redFlags: Recurrent or severe external ear infection
A solitary or atypical mass suggesting osteoma or neoplasm
reference.prognosis: The lesions are benign and slowly progressive; with water precautions and, where needed, surgical canalplasty, symptoms and complications are well controlled.
pitfalls: Confusing multiple exostoses with a solitary osteoma
Overlooking recurrent otitis externa driven by water trapping
Not advising ear protection to slow progression
Underestimating conductive hearing loss from occlusion
